chief_complaint: fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, and dry skin
hpi_details: A 32-year-old female presents to the clinic with fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, and dry skin. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: She thinks her sluggishness and dry skin are simply due to aging, winter weather, and job burnout.
concerns: She is worried that her profound exhaustion and unexplained weight gain mean she is slipping into severe clinical depression.
expectations: She hopes to have her iron and vitamin levels checked and receive practical advice or supplements to boost her energy.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Primary Hypothyroidism is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes confirming the diagnosis with TSH and free T4 before starting an individualized levothyroxine dose, with follow-up TSH in 6-8 weeks, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, and dry skin

Key HPI features: A 32-year-old female presents to the clinic with fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, and dry skin. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Primary Hypothyroidism.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Primary Hypothyroidism.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Depression without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.

Ignoring critical warning signs such as: signs of myxoedema coma (hypothermia, bradycardia, confusion, hypotension), chest pain or signs of pericardial effusion, coexisting adrenal insufficiency (unexplained hypotension, or hyponatraemia).
management_principles: Confirm the diagnosis with TSH and free T4, then start an individualized levothyroxine dose and recheck TSH in 6-8 weeks
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

source_refs.title: American Thyroid Association (ATA) Guidelines for the Treatment of Hypothyroidism

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with chief complaint of fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, and dry skin. HPI: autoimmune thyroiditis (Hashimoto).
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Primary Hypothyroidism.
reference_soap.assessment: Primary Hypothyroidism, likely autoimmune (Hashimoto's), given the fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, and dry skin — pending confirmatory TSH and free T4.
reference_soap.plan: Confirm primary hypothyroidism with TSH and free T4 before treatment and review medication interactions and pregnancy status. Start levothyroxine at an individualized dose based on age, body size, cardiac disease, and severity; recheck TSH about 6-8 weeks after initiation or dose changes.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Primary Hypothyroidism
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Primary Hypothyroidism
Implement evidence-based management plan: Levothyroxine replacement, check TSH in 6-8 weeks

teaching.one_liner: Autoimmune thyroiditis causing fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, and dry skin.
red_flags: Signs of myxoedema coma (hypothermia, bradycardia, confusion, hypotension) — a medical emergency requiring urgent IV levothyroxine and steroids
Chest pain or signs of pericardial effusion — hypothyroidism can cause pericardial effusion and unmask underlying cardiac disease
Coexisting adrenal insufficiency (unexplained hypotension, hyponatraemia) — must be excluded/treated before starting levothyroxine to avoid precipitating adrenal crisis

must_ask.say: How long has this been going on?
Do you feel cold when others don't?
How much weight have you gained?

history.answer: I've been feeling completely exhausted for the past two months, and I've also gained weight even though I'm not eating any more than usual.
It feels like a heavy lack of energy and general sluggishness throughout my whole body, rather than just being sleepy or having weak muscles.
It started gradually about two to three months ago, and there was no specific illness or life event that triggered it.
It makes it really hard to get through my workday, and resting or sleeping extra on weekends doesn't make me feel any better.
I feel worn out and sluggish all day long from the moment I wake up, with no particular time of day feeling better or worse.
I sleep about eight hours every night, but I still wake up feeling unrefreshed. I don't snore or stop breathing in my sleep.
My mood has been a bit down because of how tired I feel, but I don't feel hopeless or depressed, and I've never had thoughts of self-harm.
No, I haven't had noticeable dizziness or shortness of breath, and my stools have been normal in color with no black or bloody stools.
My periods have become noticeably heavier and a bit more irregular over the last couple of cycles.
No, I haven't had any unusual bruising or bleeding from my gums.
Yes, I feel freezing all the time, even when everyone else around me is completely comfortable or warm.
I've gained about four kilograms over the past two months, even though my appetite has actually decreased.
Yes, I've become quite constipated lately, only having a bowel movement once every three or four days.
My skin has become noticeably dry and flaky, and my hair feels coarser and seems to be shedding more than usual.
Yes, I've had some mild tingling and numbness in my fingers, especially when I'm typing at work.
No, I haven't had excessive thirst, and I'm not urinating more often than usual.
No, my skin hasn't darkened, and I don't feel dizzy when I stand up.
I've noticed some puffiness around my eyes in the mornings and mild swelling in my lower legs by the evening.
No fever, chills, or night sweats at all.
I haven't noticed any obvious swelling or pain in my neck, although my collar feels slightly snugger lately.
No chest pain, chest tightness, or racing heartbeats.
My job has normal everyday stress, but nothing unusual. I drink one cup of coffee in the morning to try to wake up.
I was reading about my symptoms online, and I wondered if this could all be related to an underactive thyroid.
I'm really worried that I'm falling into severe depression because I just don't have the energy to get out of bed anymore.
I'm hoping you can check my blood for vitamin or iron deficiencies and give me something to restore my energy.
I have no chronic medical conditions and have always been healthy until now.
I have never had any surgeries, and I've never been hospitalized.
I don't take any prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs, or herbal supplements.
I don't have any allergies to medications, foods, or anything else.
I have never smoked cigarettes.
I only have an occasional glass of wine socially, maybe once or twice a month.
I work as an office administrator and live with my husband in an apartment.
My mother has a thyroid condition that she takes a daily pill for, but no other illnesses run in my family.
My last period started about three weeks ago.
We use condoms consistently for contraception, and there is no chance that I am pregnant.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, pulse 58 beats per minute and regular, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, temperature 36.3°C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air, BMI 25.2 kg/m².
Conjunctivae are pink without pallor; sclerae are anicteric.
Diffusely, mildly enlarged, firm, non-tender thyroid gland without discrete nodules, thrill, or audible bruit.
No palpable cervical, supraclavicular, or axillary lymphadenopathy.
Regular bradycardic rhythm with normal S1 and S2; no murmurs, gallops, or friction rubs appreciated.
Clear to auscultation bilaterally with normal vesicular breath sounds and no wheezes or crackles.
Abdomen is soft, non-distended, and non-tender without palpable organomegaly or masses.
Mild non-pitting edema present over the bilateral pretibial regions.
Skin is noticeably cool, dry, and rough, with mild coarsening of scalp hair and no hyperpigmentation.
Symmetric deep tendon reflexes with a distinctly delayed relaxation phase in the patellar and Achilles reflexes.
